1.summary: A threat is any circumstance or event with the potential to adversely affect a system; it is a possible danger that may exploit a vulnerability.
1.deeper: A threat can adversely affect a system through unauthorized access, destruction, disclosure, modification of data, or denial of service. A vulnerability is the flaw or weakness the threat may exploit. A vulnerability may be exploited by a threat, but not every threat always results in an actual attack. The STRIDE model is used for threat analysis and identification.
1.analogy: A threat is like a storm on the forecast, and a vulnerability is a crack in the roof. The storm may find the crack, but a forecast storm does not always reach the house.
1.scenario: An Airman lists events that could adversely affect a network: someone gaining unauthorized access, data being modified or disclosed, files being destroyed, or service being denied. Each is a threat. Whether any of them becomes an actual attack depends on the system and its weaknesses.
1.example: A wet floor in a hallway is a possible danger to anyone who walks by, even before anyone slips. A threat is a possible danger in the same way. In the course: A threat is a possible danger that may exploit a vulnerability, Block Text p.3.

picture.alt: A threat reaches a system with a vulnerability; exploiting it, the threat can reach data, give unauthorized access or deny service to users.

1.summary: STRIDE is the model Microsoft uses for threat analysis and identification; it names six threats that system design aims to prevent.
1.deeper: STRIDE is the model Microsoft uses for threat analysis and identification, and it is a goal of system design to prevent its six threats. Spoofing is pretending to be something or someone other than yourself. Tampering is modifying something on a disk, network, memory or elsewhere. Information disclosure is providing information to someone not authorized to have it. Denial of Service is exhausting resources needed to provide services to the user. Elevation of privilege is allowing someone to do something they are not authorized to do. Repudiation, the R, is claiming you didn't do something or were not responsible. It is not spoofing, which pretends to be someone else, and not tampering, which modifies something: repudiation denies an act, or the responsibility for it.
1.analogy: STRIDE works like a checklist with six boxes. A designer walks through each box in turn and asks whether the system could fall to that threat. One box, repudiation, is like a person who signs for a delivery and later says they never signed.
1.scenario: An Airman reviews a system design and asks six questions, one per letter: could someone pretend to be another user, modify data, deny an act, see information they should not, exhaust the system's resources, or do something they are not authorized to do? Those six questions are STRIDE.
1.example: A pilot's preflight checklist makes sure no item is forgotten by naming each one. STRIDE does the same for threats, with one letter for each. In the course: The model Microsoft uses for threat analysis and identification is called STRIDE, Block Text p.3.

picture.alt: An attacker, a user, a system, its data, an unauthorized person and a restricted area; each step shows one STRIDE threat in action.

1.summary: An inside attack is initiated by an insider: an entity inside a security perimeter that has authorization to access a system but uses it in a way not approved.
1.deeper: Inside and outside attacks are two kinds of threat agent. An insider is an entity inside the security perimeter; insider threats have authorization to access a system, but they use their authorization in a way that is not approved by the party that granted it. An outside attack is initiated by an outsider, an entity outside the security perimeter, and outsider threats gain unauthorized or illegitimate access. Botnets are utilized in outside attacks.
1.analogy: An inside attack is like a staff member with a key to the stockroom who takes goods home. The key was given on purpose; the way it is used was never approved.
1.scenario: An Airman holds an approved account on a unit's system. The Airman uses that account to copy files in a way the party that granted the account never approved. Because the Airman is inside the security perimeter and has authorization, this is an inside attack.
1.example: A house sitter is given a key to water the plants, then throws a party in the house. The key was granted, but not for that use. In the course: Insider threats have authorization to access a system, but they use their authorization in a way that is not approved by the party that granted authorization, Block Text p.4.

answers.text: A Denial of Service attack

1.summary: A botnet is an aggregation of compromised computers, turned into robots used by attackers.
1.deeper: A bot, short for robot, is an automated program that executes commands. A botnet joins many compromised computers into one group of bots. Botnets are utilized in outside attacks: they are focal points for collecting stolen information, they launch automated attacks and they distribute spam. Botnets operate through a central command-and-control server and can be activated by attackers via chat rooms. A Distributed Denial of Service attack is usually performed by a botnet.
1.analogy: A botnet is like a set of puppets on strings that all lead back to one hand. Each puppet moves only when the hand pulls, and the hand is the command-and-control server.
1.scenario: Many computers on a network start sending spam at the same moment. None of their owners chose to do it: the computers were compromised and turned into bots. The commands come from one central command-and-control server that the attackers activated.
1.example: A remote control can switch on many toy robots at once from across the room. A botnet's robots are compromised computers, and the attacker holds the control. In the course: A botnet is an aggregation of compromised computers, turning them into robots used by attackers, Block Text p.4.

picture.alt: Three compromised computers (bots) run by a central command-and-control server that an attacker activates; the bots then attack a target.

steps.caption: Computers are compromised and turned into robots: bots, automated programs that execute commands.
The botnet operates through a central command-and-control server.
Attackers can activate the botnet, for example via chat rooms.
The bots launch automated attacks, distribute spam, or send the requests of a DDoS.

1.summary: A vulnerability is a flaw or weakness in a system's design, implementation, or operation and management which could be exploited to violate the system's security policies.
1.deeper: A vulnerability can lie in a system's design, its implementation, or its operation and management. A threat, a possible danger, may exploit it to violate the system's security policies. Not every threat results in an actual attack to a system, and not every attack succeeds: the degree of vulnerability, the strength of attack and the effectiveness of countermeasures determine an attack's success.
1.analogy: A vulnerability is like a window left unlatched. Nothing bad has happened yet, but it is a weak spot someone could use to get in.
1.scenario: An Airman finds that a system was designed well and built as planned, but the way it is run and looked after leaves a weakness. That weakness in operation and management is a vulnerability: a threat could exploit it to violate the system's security policies.
1.example: A bike lock with a weak link is still a lock, but the weak link is where a thief would cut. A vulnerability is that weak link in a system. In the course: A vulnerability is a flaw or weakness in a system's design, implementation, or operation and management which could be exploited to violate the system's security policies, Block Text p.4.

picture.alt: A system's design, implementation and operation; a threat attacks through the countermeasures toward the security policy.

1.summary: A network attack is an intentional act by which an intelligent threat actor attempts to evade security services and violate the security policy of a system.
1.deeper: An attack can be characterized according to intent, point of initiation and method of delivery, and it may affect one or multiple systems. Its targeted resources may include data stored in an information system (IS), services provided to the user, system processing power, any hardware, firmware or software, or even the physical design of the facility.
1.analogy: A network attack is like a burglar who studies the alarms and locks of a building before breaking in. It is planned, deliberate and aimed at getting past the defenses.
1.scenario: An Airman reviews an incident report. Someone deliberately worked around the network's security services to break the system's security policy, and the report lists the data stored on the system and the services it provides to users as the targets. That deliberate act is a network attack.
1.example: A pickpocket picks a target, chooses a moment and a method, and tries to get past the victim's guard. A network attack is just as deliberate. In the course: An attack to a network is an intentional act by which an intelligent threat actor attempts to evade security services and violate the security policy of a system, Block Text p.4.

picture.alt: A threat actor's computer linked to four kinds of targeted resource: stored data, user services, processing power and the facility design.

answers.text: Design, implementation, and operation and management

1.summary: A Denial of Service attack sends more requests to a machine than it can handle, disrupting or even totally blocking user services.
1.deeper: Denial of Service attacks are probably the nastiest and most difficult to address. They are very easy to launch and often difficult, sometimes impossible, to track because of their timing. In the example, a host can answer 20 requests per second while an attacker sends 50 per second, so the host cannot service all the attacker's requests, much less any legitimate ones. In STRIDE, Denial of Service is exhausting resources needed to provide services to the user. A standard DoS attack comes from one computer.
1.analogy: A DoS attack is like one caller dialing a help line over and over. The line is always busy, so the people who really need help cannot get through.
1.scenario: A host on an Airman's network can answer 20 requests per second. An attacker starts sending 50 per second. The host cannot service all the attacker's requests, and legitimate users get no answer at all.
1.example: A small shop can serve only so many customers at a time. If a crowd that never buys anything fills the doorway, real customers cannot get in. In the course: The intent is to send more requests to a machine than it can handle, disrupting or even totally blocking user services, Block Text p.4.

picture.alt: An attacker's computer and a user's computer both send requests to one host; the attacker's flood leaves the user unanswered.

steps.caption: The host can answer 20 requests per second.
An attacker sends 50 requests per second.
The host cannot service all the attacker's requests.
Legitimate requests go unanswered: user services are disrupted or totally blocked.

questions.stem: Why are Denial of Service attacks among the most difficult to address?

answers.text: They are very easy to launch and often difficult to track because of their timing
answers.why: DoS attacks are very easy to launch and often difficult (sometimes impossible) to track because of their timing.

answers.text: They always need a botnet of many computers
answers.why: A standard DoS attack comes from one computer; multiple computers make it a Distributed Denial of Service.

answers.text: They need an insider's authorization to start
answers.why: Nothing about a DoS attack needs authorization: its intent is to send more requests than a machine can handle.

answers.text: They change records so slightly that no one notices
answers.why: Small changes in records describe data diddling, not Denial of Service.

questions.hint: Think about how hard it is to start one, and how hard it is to find its source.
questions.takeaway: DoS attacks are easy to launch and hard to track, which makes them hard to address.

questions.stem: Put the Denial of Service example in order, from first to last.

steps.text: Legitimate requests go unanswered.
steps.why: The host cannot service the attacker's requests, much less any legitimate requests, so user services are blocked.

steps.text: An attacker sends 50 requests per second.
steps.why: The attacker sends more requests than the machine can handle.

steps.text: The host can answer 20 requests per second.
steps.why: The example starts from what the host can handle: 20 requests per second.

1.summary: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack involves multiple computers sending requests, and is usually performed by a botnet.
1.deeper: A standard DoS attack comes from one computer; a DDoS attack comes from many, as Figure 1-1 shows with a botnet. Some countermeasures may reduce the risk of DDoS attacks: not running visible-to-the-world servers at a level close to capacity, packet filtering to prevent obviously forged packets from entering the network address space, and security-related patches for host operating systems.
1.analogy: A DoS attack is one person blocking a doorway; a DDoS attack is a whole crowd pushing through the same doorway at once.
1.scenario: A server facing the outside world is flooded with requests from many computers at the same time. They are bots in a botnet. To reduce the risk next time, the Airman's unit keeps the server from running close to capacity, filters obviously forged packets and patches the host operating systems.
1.example: One person phoning a help line is a caller; hundreds of people told to phone at once can tie up every line. A DDoS attack works by numbers in the same way. In the course: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack involves multiple computers sending requests, and is usually performed by a botnet, Block Text p.5.

picture.alt: First one computer sends requests to a server (DoS); then three bots of a botnet send requests at once (DDoS).

steps.caption: A standard DoS attack comes from one computer.
A DDoS attack involves multiple computers sending requests.
A DDoS attack is usually performed by a botnet.
Countermeasures: do not run the server close to capacity, filter obviously forged packets, and patch host operating systems.

questions.stem: How does a DDoS attack differ from a standard DoS attack?

answers.text: It changes records instead of sending requests
answers.why: Changing records is data diddling. A DDoS attack still sends requests.

answers.text: It is started by an insider with authorization

answers.text: It sends fewer requests, so it is harder to see
answers.why: A DDoS attack involves multiple computers sending requests, not fewer requests.

answers.text: Multiple computers send the requests, usually a botnet
answers.why: While a standard DoS attack comes from one computer, a DDoS attack involves multiple computers and is usually performed by a botnet.

questions.hint: Count the computers on the attacking side.
questions.takeaway: DoS comes from one computer; DDoS comes from many, usually a botnet.

questions.stem: An Airman's unit must reduce the risk of DDoS attacks on its servers that are visible to the world.

steps.prompt: How heavily should those servers run?

choices.text: Close to capacity, to use every resource
choices.why: One countermeasure is not running visible-to-the-world servers at a level close to capacity.

choices.text: Not close to capacity
choices.why: Not running visible-to-the-world servers at a level close to capacity may reduce the risk of DDoS attacks.

steps.prompt: Packets arrive that are obviously forged. What should happen to them?

choices.text: Let them in and watch them
choices.why: Packet filtering should prevent obviously forged packets from entering the network address space.

choices.text: Filter them out before they enter the network address space
choices.why: Packet filtering to prevent obviously forged packets from entering the network address space is a countermeasure.

choices.text: Send them back to their source
choices.why: The countermeasure named is packet filtering to keep forged packets out, not sending them back.

steps.prompt: Security-related patches are available for the host operating systems. What should the unit do?

choices.text: Apply them
choices.why: Security-related patches for host operating systems are a countermeasure that may reduce the risk of DDoS attacks.

choices.text: Leave them, since patches do not affect DDoS risk
choices.why: Security-related patches for host operating systems are listed as a DDoS countermeasure.

questions.takeaway: Keep public servers below capacity, filter forged packets and patch host operating systems to reduce DDoS risk.

1.summary: The goal of unauthorized access attacks is to access a resource that a machine should not provide the attacker.
1.deeper: These attackers may falsely identify as the originating host. For example, if a host is a web server that provides requested web pages to the user, they may encapsulate the original data package and attach a command shell to gain access. They often accomplish this through vulnerable system areas.
1.analogy: Unauthorized access is like slipping a note into a delivery that a building already accepts, so the note gets past the front desk along with the parcel.
1.scenario: A web server provides requested web pages to users. An attacker wraps the original data package and attaches a command shell to it, working through a vulnerable area of the system. The goal is to reach a resource the web server should never provide to the attacker.
1.example: A visitor badge lets a guest into the lobby, but a guest who sneaks into the server room is using the building in a way it was never meant to allow. Reaching what you should not reach is the point of unauthorized access. In the course: The goal of these attacks is to access a resource that a machine should not provide the attacker, Block Text p.5.

picture.alt: A web server answers a user's request; an attacker sends a data package with a command shell attached and reaches a resource the server should not provide.

The attacker may falsely identify as the originating host.

1.summary: User access is one of the two main classifications of system access: selected configuration and operational control in areas such as email, share drives and files that the administrator allows.
1.deeper: Systems are divided into two main classifications of users and their system access capability: user access and administrator access. This helps keep unknown or untrusted individuals from gaining access to equipment. User access has selected control over the areas the administrator allows. With administrator rights, a person has full access to all the hardware, software and firmware operations that control cyber operations.
1.analogy: User access is like a hotel room key: it opens your room and the shared areas you are allowed to use. The manager's master key, like administrator access, opens everything.
1.scenario: An Airman with user access can use email, share drives and the files the administrator allows. When the Airman needs a change to firmware operations that control cyber operations, that is outside user access: it needs administrator rights.
1.example: On a shared family computer, a child's account may open only the games and folders a parent allows, while the parent's account can change everything. User access is the limited account. In the course: User access has selected configuration and operational control over the system in areas such as email, share drives, and files that the administrator allows them to utilize, Block Text p.5.

1.summary: Among destructive types of break-ins and attacks there are two major categories: data diddling and data destruction.
1.deeper: One category involves changing the format and the other is getting rid of the format. Data diddling occurs when an attacker makes small changes or entries in records to change the original meaning. Data destruction is destroying the data stored on tapes, hard disks and other electronic media so that it is completely unreadable. Some attackers just like to delete things, and then computing and mission capability are greatly reduced or stopped.
1.analogy: Destructive behavior is like what can happen to a library book: someone can quietly change a few words on a page, or tear the book apart so no one can read it.
1.scenario: An Airman reviews two break-ins. In the first, an attacker made small changes to entries in financial records. In the second, an attacker made the data on a hard disk completely unreadable. Both are destructive behavior: the first is data diddling, the second is data destruction.
1.example: A school report card can be harmed in two ways: someone can change one grade, or someone can shred the whole card. Destructive attacks on data fall into the same two kinds. In the course: Among destructive types of break-ins and attacks, there are two major categories: data diddling and data destruction, Block Text p.5.

1.summary: Data diddling occurs when an attacker makes small changes or entries in records to change the original meaning.
1.deeper: It is a form of computer fraud involving the intentional falsification of numbers in data entry, most often the inflation or understatement of income or expenses to benefit a company or individual on tax or other financial documents. It can be performed by malware, by someone remotely hacking into the system, or by someone manually in a data entry position. Data diddling is likely the worst type of attack because the break-in might not be immediately obvious: an accounting audit might turn up a discrepancy three or four months later. Tracking the problem down is difficult, and then it is hard to trust any numbers from that time.
1.analogy: Data diddling is like someone quietly moving the decimal point in a few lines of a ledger. Nothing looks broken, so nobody notices until the totals stop adding up.
1.scenario: An accounting audit finds a discrepancy in a unit's books from months earlier. Someone had made small changes to entries to change their meaning. Tracking down the change is difficult, and the Airman reviewing the books now asks how far back any number can be trusted.
1.example: If someone changes a single score on a sports results sheet, the sheet still looks complete, and the error may not surface until the season totals are checked. In the course: Data diddling occurs when an attacker makes small changes or entries in records to change the original meaning, Block Text p.6.

1.summary: Data destruction is the process of destroying the data stored on tapes, hard disks and other forms of electronic media so that it is completely unreadable.
1.deeper: Its objective is to ensure the data is completely unreadable and cannot be accessed or used in the system. Some attackers just like to delete things, and then computing and mission capability are greatly reduced or stopped. Examples include erasing the recycle bin, overwriting data to change the entire format, degaussing (a magnetic field that erases data and causes irreversible damage), destroying hard drives with special software, and electronic shredding (physically destroying the entire system equipment). When data is destroyed for authorized purposes, it must be completely sanitized, regardless of the method, so it cannot be accessed, recovered or used. The process varies by equipment type, classification and scenario and is explained in the sanitation disposal policy.
1.analogy: Data destruction is like running a page through a shredder: the paper may still exist, but the words on it can never be read again.
1.scenario: An Airman's unit retires old hard disks. Before they leave, the data on them must be completely sanitized so it cannot be accessed, recovered or used for unauthorized purposes. The unit follows the sanitation disposal policy for that equipment type and classification.
1.example: Before an old phone is given away, its owner wipes it so no one can read the photos and messages left on it. Making stored data completely unreadable is data destruction. In the course: The term data destruction can be defined as the process of destroying the data stored on tapes, hard disks, and other forms of electronic media so that it is completely unreadable, Block Text p.6.

Electronic shredding physically destroys the entire system equipment.
Data destroyed for authorized purposes must be completely sanitized, regardless of the method, so it cannot be accessed, recovered or used.
The process varies by equipment type, classification or scenario and is explained in the sanitation disposal policy.

1.summary: Social engineering is a non-technical or low-technology confidence trick ("con") used for attacking information systems, often involving trickery or fraud.
1.deeper: It involves psychological manipulation of people into divulging confidential information or performing other actions beneficial to an attacker, which is why it is commonly known as "hacking the human." Its purpose can be information gathering, fraud or system access. It differs from a traditional con in that it is often one of many steps in a more complex scheme. Its types include phishing, spear phishing, whaling and baiting. The best countermeasures involve educating yourself and your co-workers; others are treating unsigned email with more suspicion and verifying it with its originator, multifactor authentication, keeping antivirus and antimalware up to date, and researching any offer that looks too good to be true.
1.analogy: Social engineering is like a con artist who never picks the lock but talks the guard into opening the door.
1.scenario: An Airman receives an email that is not signed and offers something that looks too good to be true. Instead of clicking, the Airman treats it with suspicion, verifies it with its originator, and researches the offer before taking any action.
1.example: A stranger at the door says they are from the gas company and need to come in. If the homeowner lets them in without checking, the trick worked on the person, not the lock. In the course: Social engineering is a non-technical or low-technology confidence trick ("con") used for attacking information systems, often involving trickery or fraud, Block Text p.6.

picture.alt: An attacker manipulates a person, who then gives information or access to an information system; education is the best countermeasure.

1.summary: Phishing is a category of social engineering that attempts to acquire sensitive data through fraudulent solicitation via email, text messages or websites.
1.deeper: The sensitive data can be bank account numbers, passwords, email accounts and the like. A perpetrator masquerades as a legitimate business or reputable person, often broadcasting messages to a wide audience of targets or individuals within an organization. Picture a fisherman casting a line into the water with a baited hook, waiting for a victim to bite. Spear phishing is a type of phishing that targets a specific group or person, and whaling is a form of spear phishing aimed at high-value individuals.
1.analogy: Phishing is like a fisherman casting a baited line into the water: the line is not aimed at one fish, it waits for whichever one bites.
1.scenario: Many Airmen in an organization receive the same email. It looks like it comes from a legitimate business and asks each reader to enter their password on a website. The message was broadcast to a wide audience, hoping someone bites: that is phishing.
1.example: A flyer slipped under every door on a street promises a prize to anyone who calls and gives their bank details. It is sent to everyone, hoping a few respond. In the course: Phishing techniques attempt to acquire sensitive data, such as bank account numbers, passwords, email accounts, etc., through fraudulent solicitation via email, text messages, or websites, Block Text p.7.

1.summary: Multifactor authentication protects an account with more than one factor, such as a username/password combined with biometrics like a thumb print.
1.deeper: Authentication factors fall into categories: something you know (a password or PIN, the most common), something you have (a swipe card, a token or a code sent by text message), something you are (a fingerprint, voice, retina or face, which needs a biometrics system), somewhere you are, and something you do. Multifactor authentication uses two or more factors, such as a token plus a password, and is more secure than single-factor authentication. Combining things from the same category is not multifactor: a username plus a password is still two kinds of something you know. As a countermeasure against social engineering, it protects an account even when one factor is compromised, because the attacker would be less likely to have compromised all factors. A username/password combined with a thumb print is two factor authentication.
1.analogy: It is like a door with two different locks: a stolen key opens only one of them, and the door stays shut.
1.scenario: An attacker tricks an Airman into giving up a password. The account also asks for a thumb print, something the Airman is, and the attacker has only something the Airman knows. Because the attacker has not compromised all the factors, the account stays protected.
1.example: A locker that needs both a key and a code stays shut for someone who has found only the key. In the course: in the event of a system or account compromise, multifactor authentication can protect your account because the attacker would be less likely to have compromised all factors for an account, Block Text p.8.

1.summary: Malicious code is software or scripts written to intentionally cause undesired effects such as security breaches or damage to a system.
1.deeper: Malicious code is a broad category of related terms, including attack scripts, viruses, worms, Trojan horses and backdoors. A virus relies on human activity to spread, such as running an infected program. A worm is like a virus except that it needs no user intervention to self-replicate. A Trojan horse is a program a user is tricked into installing; it opens a back door that lets a hacker connect remotely and take control. The damage can be of many kinds; the imagination of the attacker is the only limitation.
1.analogy: Malicious code is like a family name: attack scripts, viruses, worms, Trojan horses and backdoors are all members of the same family, each with its own habits.
1.scenario: An Airman finds a script on a server that was written to open a security breach. Whatever its exact type, it falls under malicious code, because it was written to intentionally cause undesired effects.
1.example: A fake parking ticket left on a windshield is written on purpose to trick the driver into paying the wrong party. Code written on purpose to cause harm is malicious code. In the course: Malicious code is software or scripts written to intentionally cause undesired effects such as security breaches or damage to a system, Block Text p.8.

1.summary: Malware is software designed to infiltrate or damage a computer system without the owner's informed consent.
1.deeper: Malware is a general term for hostile, intrusive or annoying software or program code. Software counts as malware because of the perceived intent of its creator, not its features: defective software has a legitimate purpose but incidentally contains harmful bugs. Examples include viruses, worms, Trojan horses, most rootkits, spyware and dishonest adware. Most malware is written with profit in mind, and its most common pathways to users, the attack vectors, are email and the World Wide Web. Spyware is hidden software that monitors and collects information about a user and their activities, such as the websites visited, and sends it to a remote system for a hacker to review. It does not intend to damage the system; it presents a privacy threat. Adware automatically loads advertisements on the screen, typically in the form of pop-up windows.
1.analogy: Malware is like a guest who comes in pretending to visit but means to take something. What makes the guest a problem is the intent, not the coat they wear.
1.scenario: An Airman's computer shows pop-up advertisements that load on their own, and the browser is redirected to pages the Airman did not choose. Two kinds of malware may be at work: adware, which loads the advertisements, and spyware, which watches the Airman's activity and reports it to a remote system.
1.example: A sweet that someone has tampered with looks like any other sweet; the harm lies in what its maker meant it to do. Malware is judged the same way, by intent. In the course: Malware is software designed to infiltrate or damage a computer system without the owner's informed consent, Block Text p.8.

1.summary: Computer viruses are bits of code that hide in computer programs or on the boot sector of storage devices; their primary purpose is to reproduce themselves as often as possible.
1.deeper: Like a biological virus, a computer virus uses a host and spreads: it goes from PC to PC and can return to re-infect systems months or even years later. Viruses are written by people with intent to do harm, and are classified by how they propagate and how they behave: boot-sector, file infector, macro and logic bomb. They traditionally relied on human activity to spread, such as running an infected program, opening a file or inserting infected removable media. Once activated, a virus can range from simply annoying to catastrophic.
1.analogy: A biological virus infects a host and uses it as a vehicle for life, moving from person to person. A computer virus does the same with computers and programs, moving from PC to PC.
1.scenario: An Airman opens a file from a removable drive, and a virus hidden in it starts copying itself into other programs, disrupting them. That human action is how viruses traditionally spread. Months later, the same infection can come back to systems that had it before.
1.example: A cold passed around an office goes from person to person, and can come back around later. In the course: computer viruses are bits of computer programming, or code, that hide in computer programs or on the boot sector of storage devices, Block Text p.9.

picture.alt: An infected computer, the computer it spreads to, and the four virus types: boot sector, executable file, macro file and a set date.

1.summary: A Trojan horse is a program a user is tricked into installing; it works as expected but carries hidden software inside the legitimate code.
1.deeper: The software the user meant to download works exactly as expected. The extra software embedded in the legitimate code is something the user does not know about and would not give permission to install. Trojan horses allow unauthorized access to an infected host by opening a back door, which lets a hacker connect to the system remotely and take control of it.
1.analogy: It is like a gift box that holds the present you wanted, plus someone hidden underneath who unlocks your door once you are not looking.
1.scenario: An Airman installs a free program that does exactly what it promised. Hidden in its code is additional software that opens a back door. Later, a hacker connects to the Airman's computer remotely and takes control of it.
1.example: A free tote bag that carries your shopping fine but has a hidden tracker sewn into the lining does its job and something else you never agreed to. In the course: a Trojan horse is a program that a user is tricked into installing, with additional software embedded inside the legitimate code, Block Text p.10.

1.summary: A worm is like a virus, except that worms require no user intervention to self-replicate.
1.deeper: Viruses traditionally relied on human activity to spread, such as running an infected program, opening a file or inserting infected removable media. Worms need no user intervention to copy themselves. Worms can infect a network in several ways: by using certain vulnerable network ports/protocols, through infected e-mail messages that are opened, and through infective flash drives inserted into the host computer.
1.analogy: A virus is like a seed that needs someone to carry it to new ground; a worm is like a weed that spreads its own runners with no one's help.
1.scenario: No one on the network ran a program or opened a file, yet copies of the same malware appear on computer after computer. It entered through a vulnerable network port and kept copying itself. That self-replication without user intervention is what marks a worm.
1.example: A chain message that forwards itself to everyone, without anyone pressing send, spreads with no one's help. In the course: a worm is like a virus except that worms require no user intervention to self-replicate, Block Text p.10.

picture.alt: A host computer and the ways a worm infects a network: vulnerable ports/protocols, e-mail and flash drives.

1.summary: Vulnerability scanning mimics malicious network activity that hosts could encounter on a network, so routine results identify hosts that are vulnerable to attacks.
1.deeper: Vulnerability scanning is a preventative measure. The scan itself repairs nothing: it acts like an attack to see which hosts would fall to one. System administrators then remediate the vulnerabilities it finds, by patching or by otherwise changing system configurations.
1.analogy: It is like a fire drill: a pretend emergency shows which exits are blocked, so they can be cleared before a real fire.
1.scenario: MSgt Rush has the network scanned routinely. The scan mimics malicious network activity, and this week's results identify one host as vulnerable to attack. The system administrator remediates it by patching the host and changing its configuration.
1.example: A practice test shows which questions a student would get wrong before the real exam, so those topics can be studied. In the course: vulnerability scanning mimics malicious network activity that hosts could encounter on a network; routine scanning results identify hosts that are vulnerable to attacks, Block Text p.12.

1.summary: Patching is the process of repairing a vulnerability or a flaw that is identified after the release of an application.
1.deeper: Newly released patches can fix bugs, enhance applications with new features, and fix security vulnerabilities. Unpatched software can make the device a vulnerable target for exploits, so regularly patching software is critical for denying malware access to a computer/network. Patching is a preventative measure, and it is one way system administrators remediate vulnerabilities that scanning finds.
1.analogy: Patching is like mending a hole found in a fence after it was built: until it is mended, anything can slip through.
1.scenario: A vulnerability scan shows that a host runs an application with a flaw found after its release. The system administrator applies the newly released patch, which fixes the security vulnerability. Left unpatched, the host would stay a vulnerable target for exploits.
1.example: A recalled toy gets a repair kit after it is already in stores, to fix a problem found after release. In the course: patching is the process of repairing a vulnerability or a flaw that is identified after the release of an application, Block Text p.12.

1.summary: A firewall restricts data communication traffic to and from a network it is connected to, protecting network resources from outside threats.
1.deeper: A firewall protects systems on one side of it from outside systems on the other side. It monitors the data packets that reach it and either allows each one through or blocks it, following rules the administrators set. By default, administrators should configure a firewall to block all traffic, then add exceptions that specifically allow traffic through. Firewalls can be hardware, software or both: a hardware-based (network-based) firewall sits at the edge of a network, while a software-based (host-based) firewall is installed on a single system to protect that one system; NAC can check whether a host-based firewall is installed and running. A good firewall system can also block internal users from resources they have no need to know about. Firewalls are a preventative measure, like software patching and proxy servers, which are often used as part of a firewall; anti-virus and monitoring logs are detection measures.
1.analogy: A firewall is like a gate guard at the only road into a base: traffic in and out has to pass the gate, and the guard turns away what is not allowed.
1.scenario: An Airman sets up the firewall for an Internet-facing web server. The firewall starts by blocking all traffic; the Airman then adds exceptions for TCP ports 443 (HTTPS) and 80 (HTTP), the ports web server traffic runs on. Every other packet that reaches the firewall is blocked.
1.example: A front desk that checks everyone coming in and going out of a building controls who and what passes. In the course: a firewall restricts data communication traffic to and from a network it's connected to, Block Text p.12.

picture.alt: Outside traffic meets a firewall at the edge of a network; an administrator's rules block it by default and allow exceptions; a host-based firewall guards one computer inside.

1.summary: A proxy resides between a user's computer and the Internet and provides security, privacy and web filtering.
1.deeper: Proxy servers, also called web content filters, are listed with the preventative measures. Because the proxy sits between the user's computer and the Internet, it can provide security, privacy and web filtering for that traffic. Proxy servers are often used as part of a firewall, which Unit 3, Firewalls, covers.
1.analogy: A proxy is like a receptionist who takes all your outside calls: callers reach the receptionist, not you, and some calls are screened out.
1.scenario: An Airman's unit wants web filtering for its users. Their computers reach the Internet through a proxy server, which sits between them and the Internet and provides security, privacy and web filtering. The proxy is part of the unit's firewall.
1.example: A mail room that receives every package before it reaches the offices can screen what comes in. In the course: a proxy resides between a user's computer and the Internet; it provides security, privacy, and web filtering, Block Text p.12.

1.summary: The demilitarized zone (DMZ) is the network area where an organization places its mail gateway, the server that sends and receives the organization's email.
1.deeper: The mail gateway in the DMZ can be set up to scan and filter out files with problematic file extensions, viruses and spam. The gateway then forwards email to the internal email server, which distributes it to internal clients. So email reaches the DMZ first and the internal network after. DMZs are covered in more depth in Unit 4, Security Zones.
1.analogy: It is like a loading dock outside a warehouse: deliveries are checked there first, and only then carried inside.
1.scenario: Email arrives for an Airman's organization. It reaches the mail gateway in the DMZ first, which filters out a virus and some spam. The gateway forwards the rest to the internal email server, which distributes it to the Airman's computer.
1.example: A school front office receives every letter and package, checks it, and only then sends it on to the classrooms. In the course: a mail gateway is a server within an organization's demilitarized zone (DMZ) that sends and receives email for the organization, Block Text p.13.

1.summary: Anti-virus software inspects the contents of each file for a virus signature and offers ways to respond to each file that matches.
1.deeper: A system can contract viruses from websites, e-mail attachments and more. A virus signature is a specific pattern that matches a malicious profile of something known to be harmful. For each file that matches a signature, the anti-virus program offers options such as removing the offending patterns, quarantining the file or deleting the file. Anti-virus is a detection measure. A program with an out-of-date signature database will not protect the system effectively, so updates should be automatic or regular.
1.analogy: Anti-virus is like a guard with a book of wanted posters: each visitor is compared against the posters, and anyone who matches is stopped.

1.summary: A supply chain consists of multiple entities, such as governments, corporations or small businesses, coordinating to get a product or products to a destination.
1.deeper: In the business world, the destination would be a customer; in the government world, it would be a governmental institution, such as a military base. In case of a hardware failure, it is important that ordered parts are received quickly and at a low cost. An attacker will look for anything available to exploit vulnerabilities in a system or process, including the supply chain, so measures must be taken to minimize vulnerabilities.
1.analogy: A supply chain is like a relay race: several runners each carry the baton part of the way, and the race is only won when it reaches the finish line.
1.scenario: A server at a military base fails, and the unit orders a replacement part. A corporation and a small business each handle part of getting that part to the base. The unit needs it received quickly and at a low cost, and every link in that chain is something an attacker could look at.
1.example: A pizza order passes from the person taking the order, to the cook, to the driver, before it reaches your door. 1.summary: Supply chain security refers to efforts to enhance the security of the supply chain, the transport and logistics system for the cargo.
1.deeper: It combines traditional practices of supply-chain management with security requirements driven by threats such as terrorism, piracy and theft. Typical activities include credentialing the participants in the supply chain, screening and validating the contents of cargo being shipped, advance notification of the contents to the destination, securing cargo while in transit with locks and tamper-proof seals, and inspecting cargo on entry.

1.scenario: Cargo is shipped to a military base. Its contents are screened and validated before shipping, and the base gets advance notification of what is coming. Locks and tamper-proof seals protect it in transit, and the cargo is inspected on entry at the base.
1.example: A sealed lunch box that is checked when packed and checked again when opened shows if anyone tampered with it on the way. 2.summary: Network Access Control (NAC) is a wired and wireless network security solution that grants access only to systems that meet predefined conditions.
2.deeper: A system that does not meet the conditions may be directed to a restricted network. The restricted network does not grant access to network resources; it lets the user become compliant and then gain access to the main network. NAC can scan a connecting system for operating system updates, antivirus software and virus definitions, and can find out whether a host-based firewall is installed and running. On a wireless network, NAC may also require users to accept terms of usage before they get access.
2.analogy: NAC is like an inspection point at a gate: each vehicle is checked before it enters. A vehicle that fails goes to a holding area where it can be fixed, and only then continues inside.
2.scenario: An Airman's laptop tries to join the network, but its virus definitions are out of date. NAC scans the laptop, finds that it does not meet the conditions, and directs it to a restricted network. There the Airman brings the laptop into compliance, and then the laptop gains access to the main network.
2.example: Some pools ask every swimmer to shower before entering; anyone who has not is sent to the showers first and then let in. In the course: NAC is a wired and wireless network security solution that allows control of access based on predefined conditions that systems must meet prior to being granted access to a network, Block Text p.16.

2.summary: Authentication is the verification process in which a system confirms that individuals are who they say they are.
2.deeper: Secured system access needs two things: individuals identify themselves, and the system verifies them. On a logon screen, typing a username is identification. Typing the password proves the identity, because only that user should know the password. A server authenticates the user by checking what the user entered against a database of users and authentication factors, such as passwords or biometric information. Factors other than passwords can also be used. In AAA, identification and authentication together make up the first A.
2.analogy: Telling a guard your name is identification. Showing the pass that only you should hold, and the guard checking it against the list, is authentication.
2.scenario: MSgt Rush logs on to a workstation. Typing his username identifies him to the system; typing his password proves he is who he says he is. The server checks what he entered against its database of users and authentication factors before he can go further.
2.example: When you pick up a parcel, saying your name is not enough: the clerk checks your ID against the name on the parcel. In the course: a system verifying that individuals are who they say they are is called authentication, Block Text p.17.

2.summary: Authentication factors are the kinds of proof a user can offer: something you know, something you have, something you are, somewhere you are, and something you do.
2.deeper: Something you know, such as a password or a PIN, is the most common factor. Something you have relies on a physical object: a swipe card, a physical token, or a code sent to a mobile phone by text message. Something you are is a physical characteristic, such as a fingerprint, voice, retina or face, and needs a biometrics system. Somewhere you are is based on location, from GPS or an IP address. Something you do is based on habits such as typing patterns, a natural signature or gait. Multifactor authentication combines two or more different factors; two things from the same category, such as a username and a password, are still one kind: something you know.
2.analogy: The factors are like different ways to show you belong at a club: knowing the password, holding a membership card, being recognized by face, being at the right door, or signing in your usual way.
2.scenario: An Airman logs on with a password, then enters a code that was sent to a mobile phone by text message. The password is something you know; the code is something you have. Because the two come from different factors, this is multifactor authentication.
2.example: A bank card and its PIN work together: one is a thing you carry, the other a thing you remember. In the course: users can be authenticated against various kinds of authentication factors other than passwords, Block Text p.17.

2.summary: With single sign-on (SSO), users authenticate once onto a network and are granted access to multiple systems without providing additional credentials.
2.deeper: Traditionally, every server on a network requires its own logon and authentication process. SSO helps both sides. Users do not have to remember credentials for multiple systems, and administrators do not have to manage multiple logon credentials for every user on each server. The drawback: if an account is compromised, a hacker can access multiple servers rather than just one.
2.analogy: SSO is like a wristband at a fair: you show your ticket once at the gate, and the wristband gets you on every ride. Lose control of the wristband, though, and someone else gets on every ride too.
2.scenario: An Airman logs on to the network once in the morning and then opens three different servers without typing any more credentials. That is SSO. If the Airman's account were compromised, a hacker could reach all three servers, not just one.
2.example: One key ring that opens every door in a building saves carrying many keys, but losing it opens every door. In the course: with single sign-on, users authenticate once onto a network, and are granted access to multiple systems without needing to provide additional credentials, Block Text p.17.

2.summary: 802.1X is a popular authentication protocol that hardens a network: anyone who connects must provide valid credentials before the network connection is allowed.
2.deeper: An IEEE 802.1X-compliant switch can be configured together with an authentication service, so that connecting clients are authenticated before network access is permitted. The switch does not decide alone; the authentication service checks the credentials. 802.1X can be used together with RADIUS on wireless networks and on switches that support it. With RADIUS, the RADIUS server either verifies or rejects the credentials, granting or denying access.
2.analogy: 802.1X is like a door that stays locked until the front desk confirms your badge: the door does not decide by itself, it asks the desk.
2.scenario: An Airman plugs a laptop into an 802.1X-compliant switch. Before any network connection is allowed, the switch works with the authentication service to check the Airman's credentials. With valid credentials the connection is allowed; without them it is not.
2.example: A parking gate that opens only after the office confirms your permit works the same way: no confirmation, no entry. In the course: 802.1X is a popular authentication protocol for hardening a network to ensure that anyone who connects to the network provides valid credentials before the network connection is allowed, Block Text p.18.

2.summary: Systems that centralize authentication, authorization and accounting are known as "Triple A" (AAA); they are used on corporate networks, for example wireless and virtual private networks.
2.deeper: The first A is identification and authentication: the user presents information such as a username or a smartcard, and the service validates it against a database of users and authentication factors. The second A is authorization: after the account information is verified, the user is granted access to the network and can perform the tasks they have been permitted to perform. The third A is accounting: it logs user activity and tracks usage, such as access time and bandwidth. Authentication methods that serve AAA include RADIUS, Diameter and TACACS+.
2.analogy: AAA is like the entry system of a secure building: the front desk checks who you are, your badge decides which rooms you may enter, and a log records when you came and went.
2.scenario: An Airman connects to a corporate virtual private network. The AAA service validates the Airman's username and password, grants access to the tasks the Airman is permitted to perform, and logs the session's access time and bandwidth.
2.example: A gym checks your membership card at the door, lets you use only the areas your plan covers, and records each visit. In the course: systems that provide centralization of authentication, authorization, and accounting are known as "Triple A" (AAA), Block Text p.18.

2.deeper: Authorization is the second A of AAA. Authorization then covers what that verified user may do: access to the network and the permitted tasks. Accounting, the third A, logs the user's activity and usage.

2.summary: TACACS+ is the AAA protocol used in modern Cisco networks; it replaced TACACS and XTACACS.
2.deeper: Terminal Access Controller Access Control System (TACACS) is a legacy authentication service for Unix systems. Extended TACACS (XTACACS) is an authentication service for Cisco devices. 2.example: When a team swaps two old sign-in sheets for one new sign-in system, everyone uses the new one from then on. In the course: TACACS+ is the AAA protocol used in modern Cisco networks, Block Text p.19.

2.summary: Application security is ensuring the integrity of software: a system or network protected by many security measures can be undone by one unsecure application.
2.deeper: Developers must write applications securely, so that hackers cannot gain unauthorized access to a system through application vulnerabilities. Input validation ensures that entered data and pressed buttons give the desired result, leaving no keyboard characters open to manipulation. Once software is in use, best practices are: apply software patches to applications and operating systems, configure applications with security in mind (a configuration baseline), disable application features that are not necessary (application hardening), and prevent cross-site request forgery.
2.analogy: A house with strong locks on every door is still open if one window is left unlatched; one unsecure application is that window.
2.scenario: MSgt Rush runs a well-protected network, but one application on it has not been kept up to date with security patches. Its vulnerabilities put the rest of the security at risk. Patching it, configuring it with security in mind and disabling the features users do not need restores the integrity of the software.
2.example: A strong front-door lock does little good if a back window is left open. In the course: application security is ensuring the integrity of software, Block Text p.19.

2.summary: A software development life cycle (SDLC) outlines how an application is developed; it is divided into phases, whose number and type depend on the SDLC model.
2.deeper: The common SDLC phases are: requirements gathering and analysis (what the application is supposed to do), design (from those requirements), implementation (the code is written), testing (the code is checked for functionality, including fuzzing: random invalid data entered into input fields to find crashes, memory leaks and other bugs), deployment (installing the application on the production servers), and maintenance (users give feedback and reported problems are fixed). Two SDLC models are Waterfall and Agile.
2.analogy: An SDLC is like building a house: decide what the owners need, draw the plans, build, inspect, hand over the keys, and fix what the owners report later.
2.scenario: An Airman's team is building a new application. They first gather what it must do, design it, and write the code. In testing, they enter random invalid data into the input fields to look for crashes. Then they install it on the production servers, and later fix the problems users report.
2.example: A recipe is planned, written, tried out in the kitchen, served, and then adjusted when diners comment. In the course: the development process of an application is outlined in a software development life cycle (SDLC), Block Text p.19.

2.summary: Application vulnerabilities are weaknesses in software that attackers can exploit, such as peer-to-peer file sharing, ActiveX controls, cookies and scripting.
2.deeper:
Developers must develop securely, so that hackers cannot gain unauthorized access to a system through application vulnerabilities. Peer-to-peer (P2P) file sharing applications share files such as music, videos and software between users, and are a common method of transmitting malicious code. Web sites and applications that use ActiveX controls can manipulate a system and obtain full system access; agreeing to run them should be discouraged. Cookies are small text files with user preferences and logon information; anyone who accesses the file can see that information.

Scripting: a script is a list of commands to be performed by a program or scripting engine. Scripts automate processes on a computer and generate web pages. They are an application security issue because they can make modifications to a system without user input. Cross-site scripting (XSS) is an attack that uses JavaScript to inject malicious code into a web application.
2.analogy: Each vulnerability is like a different unlocked entry into a building: a delivery door anyone uses, a master key handed to a stranger, a note with your passcode left on the desk, or a to-do list that an assistant carries out line by line without asking you first.
2.scenario: An Airman's browser prompts to run ActiveX controls on a website. Because ActiveX controls can obtain full system access, the Airman declines. Later the Airman finds a P2P file sharing application and a script on the workstation: the first is a common way for malicious code to arrive, and the second can change the system without anyone being asked.
2.example: A house can be entered through a door, a window, a garage or a pet flap; each opening needs its own attention. 2.summary: Cookies are small text files that websites store on client computers; they contain user preferences and logon information.
2.deeper: If someone else accesses the text file, they can see the information on it, and HTTP traffic is unencrypted and can be intercepted. Cookies also matter for cross-site request forgery: a website may contain code that references another web page that takes the user's unexpired cookies for authentication. To prevent this, users should deny "Remember Me" in the browser, and developers should set cookies to expire quickly. Cross-site scripting can also let a perpetrator steal session cookies to impersonate users.
2.analogy: A cookie is like a note a shop leaves on your desk with your preferences and sign-in details: handy for the next visit, but anyone who reads the note learns them.
2.scenario: A website offers to "Remember Me" for an Airman. Accepting would leave unexpired cookies on the computer, which code on another web page could take for authentication. The Airman denies it, and the site's developers set its cookies to expire quickly.
2.example: A coat-check ticket holds just enough for the attendant to hand back the right coat, and whoever holds it can use it. In the course: web sites store cookies (small text files) on client computers that contain user preferences and logon information, Block Text p.21.

2.summary: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a common attack that uses JavaScript to inject malicious code into a web application.
2.deeper: With XSS, hackers inject malicious code into websites. XSS can compromise user accounts, activate Trojan horse programs, mislead users into revealing private data, and enable a perpetrator to steal session cookies to impersonate users. It builds on scripting: a script is a list of commands performed by a program or scripting engine.
2.analogy: XSS is like slipping a forged page into a shop's catalog: every customer who reads the catalog gets the forger's page along with the real ones.
2.scenario: A hacker injects malicious JavaScript into a website that Airmen use. Through the injected code, the hacker steals an Airman's session cookies and uses them to impersonate the Airman on the site.
2.example: A fake notice pinned to a real notice board is trusted because of where it hangs. In the course: cross site scripting (XSS) is a common attack that uses JavaScript to inject malicious code into a web application, Block Text p.21.

2.summary: Encryption puts information in an unreadable format until an authorized person decrypts it, which places it back in cleartext, a readable format.
2.deeper: File permissions are not enough to keep data confidential. Permissions decide which user accounts can access a file on the server, but when users download files across the network, the permissions do not protect the contents from being read in transit. Files can be encrypted at two levels. In storage: if hackers get physical access, they can normally bypass permissions, but encrypted data stays unreadable. In transit: the communications channel between the two systems is encrypted, and so is the tunnel the data travels through, so someone who taps into the communication cannot read it.
2.analogy: Encryption is like writing a letter in a code only the recipient can read: anyone who catches the letter on the way, or finds it in a drawer, sees only nonsense.
2.scenario: An Airman downloads a file from a server whose permissions are set correctly. The permissions do not protect the file while it crosses the network, so the communications channel is encrypted. On the server, the file is also encrypted in storage, in case someone with physical access bypasses the permissions.
2.example: A locker's padlock keeps people out of the locker, but a diary written in a private code stays unreadable even if someone gets in. In the course: encrypting data puts the information in an unreadable format until an authorized person decrypts the data, which places it back to cleartext, Block Text p.22.

2.summary: An intrusion detection system (IDS) detects suspicious activity on a host or a network, logs it, and alerts system or network administrators.
2.deeper: An intrusion prevention system (IPS) monitors in the same way but also takes corrective action. Both come in two forms: host-based (HIDS and HIPS) and network-based (NIDS and NIPS). A HIDS displays notifications within the application or sends them by email. A NIDS is required for monitoring activity on multiple systems: it analyzes all traffic that travels across the network, logs suspicious activity and sends an administrative alert.
2.analogy: An IDS is like a security camera with a recorder and an alarm: it watches, keeps a record and calls someone, but it does not stop the intruder itself.
2.scenario: Overnight, an IDS on a network notices suspicious activity. It logs the details and alerts the network administrator, who reviews the alert in the morning. Stopping the activity would have needed an IPS.
2.example: A motion sensor that turns on a light and sends a message tells you someone is there but does not lock the door. In the course: an intrusion detection system (IDS) detects suspicious activity on a host or a network, logs it, and alerts system or network administrators, Block Text p.22.

2.summary: An intrusion prevention system (IPS) monitors hosts or networks for suspicious activity and takes corrective action.
2.deeper:
An IDS only detects suspicious activity, logs it and alerts administrators; an IPS also takes corrective action. IDSs and IPSs can be host-based (HIDS/HIPS) or network-based (NIDS/NIPS): a network-based IPS watches a network, a host-based IPS watches one host.

Host-based IPS (HIPS): it actively protects its host by stopping attacks. Compare a HIDS on the same host: it displays notifications within the application or sends them to a designated email address, and an administrator reviews them. A HIPS does not stop at notifying: it stops the attack.
2.analogy: An IDS is the referee who notes a foul; an IPS is the referee who also stops play. A network IPS referees the whole field, a host IPS guards one player.
2.scenario: An Airman must protect one workstation so that attacks on it are stopped, not just reported. An IDS would only log and alert, so the Airman needs an IPS, and because it is one host, the host-based form: a HIPS.
2.example: A lifeguard who blows the whistle and swims out does more than one who only writes down what happened. In the course: intrusion prevention systems (IPS) monitor hosts or networks for suspicious activity and take corrective action, Block Text p.22.

2.summary: A host-based intrusion detection system (HIDS) detects suspicious activity on its host and displays notifications within the application, or sends them to a designated email address.
2.deeper: An IDS detects suspicious activity, logs it and alerts administrators; a HIDS does this for one host. You review the notification events to identify any suspicious activity. When looking at the output, review the date and time of the event, the source of the event, and the account that caused it. Using this information, you decide whether a configuration change is needed. A host-based intrusion prevention system (HIPS), by contrast, actively protects the host by stopping attacks.

2.scenario: An Airman receives an email from the HIDS on a server. The Airman reviews the notification event: its date and time, its source, and the account that caused it. From that, the Airman decides whether a configuration change is needed.
2.example: A doorbell camera that sends a clip to your phone shows when, where and who; you decide what to do about it. In the course: a host-based intrusion detection system displays notifications within the application (or sends them to a designated email address), Block Text p.22.

2.summary: Within the BIOS, the complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) setup program determines which storage device the system boots from.
2.deeper: The BIOS chip holds code that interfaces with the hardware. Because CMOS decides the boot device, an attacker can insert a disc into the optical drive and boot into another operating system, bypassing the system's normal OS security controls. Best practice is to disable booting from everything but the primary storage drive. To protect the CMOS itself, a bootup password can be required before getting to the OS.
2.analogy: The CMOS boot setting is like the instruction to a building's guard about which entrance to open in the morning: if any entrance is allowed, an intruder can walk in through a side door and avoid the main checkpoint.
2.scenario: An attacker reaches an Airman's computer and inserts a disc into the optical drive. Because the CMOS setup allows booting from that drive, the system starts another operating system and the normal OS security controls are bypassed. Setting CMOS to boot only from the primary storage drive closes this path.
2.example: A car that will start for any key cut to fit is easier to take than one that starts only for its own key. In the course: within the BIOS, the CMOS setup program determines what storage device to boot the system from, Block Text p.22.

2.summary: Hardware (device) encryption is done using chips physically installed in the system, and applies very complex encryption more quickly than software encryption.
2.deeper:
Hardware encryption uses chips physically installed in the system. With full disk encryption (FDE), an entire hard disk drive is encrypted in case of theft or loss; on Windows, BitLocker performs FDE, and without the BitLocker key the system cannot boot. Permanent and removable storage devices, such as hard drives and USB drives, can and should be encrypted.

Trusted Platform Module (TPM): when FDE is used, the TPM stores the cryptographic keys used to encrypt the data. On Windows-based operating systems, BitLocker utilizes the TPM.

Hardware security module (HSM): cryptographic processors can also be stored on a separate card installed on a system. The HSM is an add-on device.
2.analogy: Hardware encryption is like a calculator chip built for one job: it does that job faster than doing the sums by hand in software. The TPM is the built-in safe for the keys; the HSM is an extra card you slot in.
2.scenario: An Airman's Windows laptop uses BitLocker for full disk encryption, and the keys used to encrypt the disk are stored in the laptop's TPM. On a server that needs more cryptographic processing, the Airman installs an HSM: a separate card added to the system.
2.example: A dishwasher built into a kitchen does its job faster than washing by hand. In the course: device encryption, or hardware encryption, applies very complex encryption more quickly than software encryption, Block Text p.23.

2.summary: Full disk encryption (FDE) encrypts an entire hard disk drive, so its contents stay protected in case of theft or loss.
2.deeper: In Windows 7 or higher, BitLocker performs FDE, encrypting the entire contents of the disk drive, including the OS. Without the BitLocker key, the system cannot boot. When FDE is used, a TPM stores the cryptographic keys used to encrypt the data. Permanent and removable storage devices, such as hard drives and USB drives, can and should be encrypted.
2.analogy: FDE is like locking an entire filing cabinet rather than single folders: whoever carries off the cabinet still cannot open any drawer without the key.
2.scenario: An Airman's laptop, protected with BitLocker FDE, is lost on a trip. Whoever finds it does not have the BitLocker key, so the system cannot boot, and the entire contents of the drive, including the OS, stay encrypted.
2.example: A safe that is carried away is still a locked safe. In the course: an entire hard disk drive can be encrypted using Full Disk Encryption (FDE) in case of theft or loss, Block Text p.23.

2.summary: A network-based intrusion detection system (NIDS) is required for monitoring activity on multiple systems; it analyzes all traffic that travels across the network.
2.deeper: A NIDS can be its own network device or software on a system. It looks for suspicious activity, logs the details and sends out an administrative alert. Its components work together. A sensor, software or hardware placed on each network segment, collects that segment's traffic and forwards it to the analysis engine, or to a collector if the infrastructure has one; the collector gathers traffic from the sensors and sends it on. The analysis engine analyzes the packets to determine whether they are suspicious. The console is where alerts and notifications are typically sent, and where the administrator configures the NIDS.
2.analogy: A NIDS is like a building's camera system: cameras in each hallway, a recorder that gathers the feeds, someone who studies them, and a control desk where the alarms ring.
2.scenario: An Airman sets up a NIDS for a network with two segments. A sensor on each segment collects its traffic and forwards it to a collector, which sends it to the analysis engine. When the engine finds suspicious packets, an alert arrives at the console, where the Airman also configures the NIDS.
2.example: A weather service gathers readings from stations across a region, studies them centrally and sends out warnings. In the course: a network-based intrusion detection system (NIDS) is required for monitoring activity on multiple systems, Block Text p.24.

3.summary: User settings are group policy configurations that apply to a user no matter which machine is used; they restrict user abilities on desktops.
3.deeper: Group policy lets network administrators change which Windows features are available to users and manage system security. A set of group policy configurations is called a group policy object (GPO). User settings follow the user to any machine. They include logon and logoff scripts, Internet Explorer settings such as favorites and the default home page, which Control Panel features users can change, which desktop icons appear and which items appear in the Start menu.
3.analogy: User settings are like a personal badge that carries the same access rules into any building the holder enters: the rules travel with the person, not with the building.
3.scenario: An Airman moves between several workstations during a shift. Because the restrictions are set as user settings, the same Control Panel limits, desktop icons and Start menu items appear on whichever machine the Airman logs on to.
3.example: A streaming account shows the same profile and parental limits on any screen where its owner signs in. User settings work the same way: they belong to the person, not the device. In the course: user settings apply to a user no matter which machine is used and are used to restrict user abilities on desktops, Block Text p.25.

3.summary: In a forward proxy, the client sends its request to the proxy server, which retrieves the resource out on the Internet and sends the response back to the client.
3.deeper: The forward proxy is the usual proxy: internal clients reach out to the Internet through it. A reverse proxy turns the direction around. It is used when a system on the Internet must send a request to one of your internal systems, such as a web server or mail server. The Internet system sends the request to the reverse proxy, which checks that the request is not malicious and then forwards it to the internal server. In both cases, all communication goes through the proxy.
3.analogy: A forward proxy is like a personal shopper you send out: you tell the shopper what you want, the shopper goes to the store and brings it back to you. A reverse proxy is like a receptionist who meets outside visitors and walks them to the right office.
3.scenario: An Airman at an internal workstation opens a web page. The request goes to the forward proxy, which fetches the page from the Internet and returns it. Later the Airman sees a different setup: a system on the Internet sends a request to the unit's internal web server through a reverse proxy.
3.example: Asking a friend who is going to the store to pick something up for you means the store deals only with your friend, who brings the item back. A forward proxy fetches resources for the client in a similar way. In the course: a forward proxy is where the client sends the request to the proxy server and the proxy retrieves the resource out on the Internet and sends the response to the client, Block Text p.27.

3.summary: An access control list (ACL) is built by setting permissions on files and folders so that only a specific group of users can access them, which maintains confidentiality.
3.deeper: ACLs come in three categories: File System ACLs, Active Directory ACLs and Networking ACLs. A File System ACL on a Windows server is set in two steps: secure the folder with NTFS permissions, then set share permissions when the folder is shared out to the network. A Networking ACL is set on a router: Cisco routers use access lists, standard or extended, to regulate traffic in and out of the network.
3.analogy: An ACL is like a guest list at a door: only the names on the list get in, so what is inside stays private to that group.
3.scenario: An Airman must keep a set of planning files readable only by one office. The Airman sets permissions on the folder so that only that office's group of users can reach it. The files stay confidential to that group.
3.example: A shared online photo album can be set so only invited family members can open it. Permissions on files and folders work the same way. In the course: implementing permissions on the files and folders is known as building an access control list (ACL), and allowing only a specific group of users access to the files maintains confidentiality, Block Text p.28.
