7.summary: A protected distribution system (PDS) is a wire line or fiber-optic telecommunication system with adequate safeguards and countermeasures that permit its use to transmit unencrypted information.
7.deeper: A PDS, sometimes called a protective distribution system or a TEMPEST system, uses acoustical, electromagnetic and physical safeguards. Its objective is to comply with TEMPEST requirements. There are two categories. A hardened distribution system (HDS) has significant physical security: the line runs in hardened conduit, an alarmed carrier or a continuously viewed carrier. A simple distribution system (SDS) has a reduced level of physical security: the cables run in a carrier of any material (wood, plastic or metal), its joints and access points are secured and controlled by personnel cleared to the highest level of data handled, and it is inspected per local policy. Which one is used depends on the classification of the information and the threat level at the facility.
7.analogy: A PDS is like an armored hallway for papers that are not in envelopes: since the papers are open, the hallway itself must keep everyone out.
7.scenario: An Airman must run a line that will carry unencrypted information. The PDS chosen depends on the classification of the information and the threat level of the facility: a hardened distribution system in hardened conduit, an alarmed carrier or a continuously viewed carrier, or a simple distribution system in a carrier of any material.
7.example: A private corridor between two secure rooms lets people carry open papers without putting them in a locked case. A PDS protects the path instead of the message. 7.summary: Red/black separation is the principle of separating signals that carry sensitive or classified plain-text information (red) from signals that carry encrypted information, or cipher-text (black).
7.deeper: The Red/Black Principle, also called red/black architecture or red/black engineering, is the careful separation and partitioning of red and black signals in cryptographic systems. It does not apply to fiber-optic cabling, because light waves do not carry an electromagnetic signal that can cause interference; it is still relevant for copper-based cabling. All TEMPEST standards require strict red/black separation, or shielding between all circuits and equipment that carry classified and non-classified data. TEMPEST-approved equipment must be built under careful quality control: changing even a single wire can invalidate the TEMPEST tests.
7.analogy: Red/black separation is like keeping raw food apart from cooked food in a kitchen: the two are kept on separate boards so the one cannot contaminate the other.
7.scenario: An Airman plans the cabling for a room where some circuits carry classified plain text and others carry cipher-text. On copper cabling, the red and black circuits must be strictly separated or shielded from each other. A fiber-optic run would not need the separation.
7.example: A clinic keeps used needles in a separate marked bin, never mixed with clean supplies. In the course: the Red/Black Principle represents the meticulous separation and partitioning in cryptographic systems of signals that contain sensitive or classified plain-text information (red signals) from those that carry encrypted information, or cipher-text (black signals), Block Text p.60.

7.summary: Information Protection (IP) is a subset of the Air Force Security Enterprise, made of three core security disciplines: Personnel Security, Industrial Security and Information Security.
7.deeper: The Air Force Security Enterprise is the organizations, infrastructure and measures (policies, processes, procedures and products) in place to safeguard Air Force personnel, information, operations, resources, technologies, facilities and assets. Within it, IP uses three disciplines. Personnel Security determines whether military, civilian and contractor personnel are eligible to access classified information or occupy a sensitive position. Industrial Security ensures the protection of classified information and controlled unclassified information (CUI) released or disclosed to industry in connection with classified contracts. Information Security protects classified information and CUI whose unauthorized disclosure could reasonably be expected to damage national security.
7.analogy: IP is like a museum’s protection plan with three teams: one checks who may enter the vaults, one watches pieces lent to outside firms, and one guards the collection itself.
7.scenario: A contractor will work on a classified contract. Personnel Security decides whether the contractor is eligible to access classified information. Industrial Security protects the classified information released to the company for the contract. Information Security protects the classified information and CUI itself.
7.example: A company that checks who may enter its records room, controls what it shares with suppliers, and guards the records themselves is protecting its information in three ways. In the course: Information Protection consists of a set of three core security disciplines (Personnel Security, Industrial Security, and Information Security), Block Text p.61.

7.summary: Since 1967, the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) has given the public the right to request access to records from any federal agency, subject to nine exemptions.
7.deeper: FOIA is often described as the law that keeps citizens in the know about their government. Federal agencies must disclose any information requested under FOIA unless it falls under one of nine exemptions, which protect interests such as personal privacy, national security and law enforcement. Agencies must also post certain categories of information online, including frequently requested records. When processing requests, agencies should withhold information only if they reasonably foresee that disclosure would harm an interest protected by an exemption, or if disclosure is prohibited by law. Exemption 1 covers information that is currently and properly classified; others cover, for example, trade secrets obtained in confidence, personal privacy, and geological information concerning wells.
7.analogy: FOIA is like a public library rule for government records: anyone may ask for a record, and the librarian hands it over unless it sits in one of a few locked sections.
7.scenario: A citizen requests records from a federal agency. The agency discloses what it holds unless an exemption applies. It withholds a classified document under Exemption 1, and releases the rest, because their disclosure would harm no interest an exemption protects.
7.example: A town that posts its meeting minutes and answers residents’ requests for records keeps them informed about their own government. In the course: since 1967, the Freedom of Information Act has provided the public the right to request access to records from any federal agency, Block Text p.61.

7.summary: CUI is government created or owned information that needs safeguarding or dissemination controls. It is unclassified: CUI is a designation, not a classification.
7.deeper: Some unclassified information needs access and distribution controls and protective measures; such information is called CUI collectively, and DoDI 5200.48 describes its types and markings. The originator of a document decides at origination whether the information may qualify for a CUI status, and determines which FOIA exemption applies. CUI may be circulated within the DoD as needed for official business, but it does not have the same protection as classified information. During working hours, reasonable steps keep unauthorized personnel from it. After hours it may be stored in unlocked containers, desks or cabinets if government or government-contract building security is provided; otherwise it goes in locked desks, file cabinets or rooms.
7.analogy: CUI is like a staff-only notice: it is not locked in the vault with the secrets, but it is not handed to everyone either. It gets handling rules, not a vault.
7.scenario: An Airman prints the unit recall roster, a list of personnel with their telephone numbers and addresses. The roster can be designated CUI under FOIA Exemption 6, because releasing it would be a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy. At the end of the day the building has government security, so the roster may go in an unlocked desk; without that building security, it would go in a locked desk or cabinet.
7.example: A clinic keeps its patient phone list behind the desk, away from the waiting room, even though the list is not a secret file. CUI is unclassified information with controls on who sees it. In the course: CUI is government created or owned information that requires safeguarding or dissemination controls consistent with applicable laws, regulations, and government wide policies, Block Text p.62.

7.summary: FOUO is a legacy marking for unclassified information that can reasonably be expected to qualify for exemption under one or more of FOIA Exemptions 2 through 9. As the CUI Program is implemented, it will cease to be an authorized marking.
7.deeper: Information must be unclassified to be designated FOUO; currently and properly classified information is withheld under FOIA Exemption 1 instead. FOUO was a DoD dissemination control under the category of CUI: all FOUO information was CUI, but not all CUI was FOUO. DoD applied it when public disclosure of a record would reasonably be expected to cause a foreseeable harm to an interest protected by Exemptions 2 through 9. Legacy documents may still carry it during the move to CUI. DoD legacy material does not have to be re-marked while it remains under DoD control, but a document shared outside DoD must be marked as CUI if the information qualifies.
7.analogy: FOUO is like an old version of a form that is being phased out: you still find it in old files, but new paperwork uses the new form, CUI.
7.scenario: MSgt Rush finds an old document marked U//FOUO on a DoD access-controlled site. While it stays under DoD control, it does not need to be re-marked. When it is to be shared outside DoD and the information qualifies as CUI, it must be marked as CUI.
7.example: An office that changes its letterhead may still find the old letterhead on letters in its files, while every new letter uses the new one. FOUO is the old marking still seen on legacy documents. In the course: For Official Use Only (FOUO) is a legacy marking used to indicate sensitivity based on agency policy or practice, Block Text p.63.

7.summary: The Privacy Act of 1974 prescribes the management, access, handling and denial of access to records within a system of records.
7.deeper: An official system of records is a file system, hard copy or digital, authorized by law or Executive Order and controlled by an Air Force or lower-level directive, that is needed to carry out an Air Force mission or function. The Act applies to personal information, such as social security number, age, military rank, civilian grade, marital status, race, salary, phone number and address, maintained in a system of records on living U.S. citizens and permanent resident aliens. It balances the government's need to keep information about individuals with their right to be protected against unwarranted invasions of privacy. The Air Force Privacy and Civil Liberties Program, implemented through AFI 33-332, sets guidelines for such information, and all Air Force personnel, civilian and military, must comply.
7.analogy: The Act is like the rules for a records office's filing cabinets: which cabinets count, what inside them is protected, whose files they are, and who has to follow the rules.
7.scenario: An Airman maintains a unit file of personnel records with names, ranks, salaries and Social Security Numbers, kept under an Air Force directive. The records sit in an official system of records on living U.S. citizens, so the Privacy Act protects them, and AFI 33-332 guides how the Airman collects, uses and shares them.
7.example: A doctor's office keeps patient files and has rules about who may see them. The Privacy Act sets rules for the personal records the government keeps. In the course: the Privacy Act of 1974 prescribes the management, access, handling, and denial of access to records within a system of records, Block Text p.64.

7.summary: Classified information has been determined to require protection against unauthorized disclosure in the interest of national defense. Its three collateral levels are Confidential, Secret and Top Secret: the greater the potential damage, the higher the protection.
7.deeper:
National security here means the defense of the United States or its foreign relations. Access needs a mission essential need, clearance eligibility, a signed SF 312 and a need to know.

Confidential needs less protection than Secret or Top Secret; its disclosure could cause some damage. It may also travel by first class mail between DoD component locations.

Secret needs a substantial degree of protection; its disclosure could cause serious damage. It may also travel by U.S. Postal Service registered mail within the 50 states.

Top Secret needs the highest degree of protection; its disclosure could cause exceptionally grave damage. Its container is under continuous guard or an alarm answered within 15 minutes.
7.analogy: The three levels are like three grades of lock on the same building: the more harm a break-in would do, the stronger the lock, and the fewer the ways to carry what it guards.
7.scenario: MSgt Rush hands an Airman three folders. The Confidential one may go by first class mail to another DoD component location. The Secret one goes by registered mail, in two opaque, sealed envelopes. The Top Secret one goes only by an approved TS crypto system or by cleared U.S. military personnel designated to carry it, and is stored in a TS-approved container under guard or an alarm answered within 15 minutes.
7.example: A bank keeps loose change in a drawer, cash in a locked safe and its most valuable holdings in a guarded vault: the bigger the possible loss, the stronger the protection. In the course: classified information is information that has been determined to require protection against unauthorized disclosure in the interest of national defense, Block Text p.64.

7.summary: The General Services Administration (GSA) establishes and publishes standards and specifications for storage devices that safeguard classified material.
7.deeper: Classified information must be secured under conditions adequate to prevent access by unauthorized persons. Top Secret goes in a GSA security container approved for Top Secret, under continuous protection by guard or duty personnel or an intrusion detection system with a response within 15 minutes; Secret and Confidential go in a GSA security container approved for the appropriate level. Weapons and sensitive items such as funds, jewels, precious metals or drugs are not stored in the same container used for classified information. When the size or nature of some classified material makes GSA approved containers unsuitable, secure rooms may be built, and they must be approved by the Information Security Program Manager. COMSEC materials are stored in a GSA approved safe of the appropriate classification.
7.analogy: GSA works like the author of a building code for safes: it does not guard your papers itself, but every approved container has to meet its standard.
7.scenario: An Airman finds unit funds placed in the container that holds Secret documents. Funds may not share a container used for classified information, so they are moved out. A large classified item will not fit in any GSA approved container, so a secure room approved by the Information Security Program Manager is used instead.
7.example: A building code says how strong a fire door must be, and builders follow it. GSA plays that standard-setting role for storage devices. In the course: the General Services Administration (GSA) establishes and publishes standards and specifications for storage devices, Block Text p.69.

7.summary: OPSEC is a process of identifying, analyzing and controlling critical information to reduce the vulnerability of Air Force missions by eliminating or reducing successful adversary collection and exploitation.
7.deeper: OPSEC applies to all activities that prepare, sustain or employ forces during all phases of operations. A vulnerability exists when the adversary can collect critical information or indicators, analyze them and act quickly enough to impact friendly objectives. Air Force organizations integrate OPSEC into mission planning; program responsibility can be delegated to lower-level squadron personnel, but the Commander retains responsibility for risk management decisions and the overall implementation of countermeasures. OPSEC is the responsibility of all AF personnel, it is a continuous process, and failure to implement directed OPSEC measures will be considered for disciplinary action.
7.analogy: OPSEC is like a card player who first decides which cards matter, then notices which habits could give them away, and then changes those habits.
7.scenario: A squadron plans an exercise. Its planners record the critical information and indicators in a CIIL, look at which of the unit's actions adversary intelligence could observe, work out what could be collected and interpreted in time to be useful to an adversary, and then select and carry out measures that reduce those vulnerabilities to an acceptable level.
7.example: A family away on holiday might stop the newspaper delivery so a pile on the doorstep does not show that the house is empty. OPSEC thinks the same way about what others can observe. In the course: OPSEC is a process of identifying, analyzing, and controlling critical information indicating friendly actions associated with military operations and other activities, Block Text p.71.

picture.alt: The OPSEC process: list critical information, see what an adversary can observe, judge what it reveals, then apply measures.

Determine what indications could be collected, analyzed and interpreted to derive critical information in time to be useful.
Select and execute measures that eliminate or reduce the vulnerabilities to an acceptable level.

7.summary: Critical information is a fact about friendly intentions, capabilities and activities that adversaries vitally need to plan and act effectively against friendly mission accomplishment.
7.deeper: Recording critical information and indicators in a critical information and indicators list (CIIL) is the product of the first step of the OPSEC process. Critical information is best identified by the individuals responsible for planning and executing the organization's mission. Once a CIIL is developed, commanders must approve the list and ensure the information is protected or controlled. It is identified at the earliest stages of planning an operation or activity and continuously updated as necessary. All AF personnel must know their organization's critical information and protect it in letters, resumes, articles, email, social media and blog postings, message boards and other forms of dissemination.
7.analogy: Critical information is like the play a team will run next: the other side needs it to plan, so the coaches who design the play decide what to keep quiet, and the head coach signs off.
7.scenario: At the first planning meeting for an operation, the people who will plan and execute it list what an adversary would vitally need to know about the unit's intentions, capabilities and activities. They record it in the CIIL, the commander approves the list, and the planners update it as the plan changes.
7.example: A company may keep its product launch date quiet because a rival could use it to plan. Critical information is the fact an adversary needs in order to plan and act. In the course: critical information is a fact about friendly intentions, capabilities, and activities vitally needed by adversaries for them to plan and act effectively, Block Text p.72.

7.summary: An indicator is a friendly detectable action and open-source information that an adversary can interpret or piece together to derive critical information.
7.deeper: Indicators are recorded with critical information in the critical information and indicators list (CIIL). The adversary uses what it derives to support its own decision-making; it has then exploited a friendly vulnerability to gain an advantage. A vulnerability exists when the adversary can collect critical information or indicators, analyze them and act quickly enough to impact friendly objectives. Encrypting email that holds critical information or OPSEC indicators is one protective measure, but with personal electronic devices in common use, adversaries do not need expensive measures to learn ample information about operations.
7.analogy: Indicators are like puzzle pieces: one piece shows little, but enough pieces fitted together reveal the picture.
7.scenario: Several Airmen each share a small, separate detail in public: a farewell post here, a packing photo there. None is critical information by itself, but an adversary can piece these detectable actions together to derive that the unit is about to move, and use that in its own planning.
7.example: Lights left on late every night in a shop's back office can tell a rival that something big is coming. An indicator is that kind of visible clue. In the course: an indicator is a friendly detectable action and open-source information that can be interpreted or pieced together by an adversary to derive critical information, Block Text p.72.

7.summary: Social media is one of the easiest ways for adversaries to gather information about military operations, so critical or sensitive information is kept off it.
7.deeper: Do not publicly post photographs that display critical or sensitive information, such as IED strikes, battle scenes, casualties, destroyed or damaged equipment, personnel killed in action and the protective measures of military facilities. This includes websites such as Instagram, Twitter, Facebook and other social media sites or applications. OPSEC vulnerabilities can be online or in person: an open conversation online may be a Facebook wall or public Twitter posts. Even private messaging features carry a potential for interception and eavesdropping, and you may not know all your online followers or friends as well as you think.
7.analogy: A social media post is like a note pinned to a public notice board: once it is up, you do not choose who stops to read it.
7.scenario: An Airman back from deployment wants to share photos. A picture of destroyed equipment and one showing a facility's protective measures stay off social media. A post about the next deployment that names the departure date and destination would be a breach of operations security.
7.example: A note left on a public notice board can be read by anyone who walks past, not only the friends it was meant for. A social media post works the same way. In the course: one of the easiest ways for our adversaries to gather information about military operations is through social media, Block Text p.72.

7.summary: COMSEC is the program of measures and controls that denies unauthorized persons information derived from U.S. Government information systems related to national security, and ensures the authenticity of those systems.
7.deeper: COMSEC is a Cyber Security discipline outlined in AFI 17-130, Cybersecurity Program Management. Its protection results from applying cryptosecurity and transmission security to communications and information systems that generate, handle, store, process or use classified or sensitive government information, the loss of which could adversely affect the national security interest; it also includes physical security measures for COMSEC information or materials. Because of a wide variety of vulnerabilities, COMSEC is subdivided into three manageable components: cryptosecurity, transmission security (TRANSEC) and physical security.
7.analogy: COMSEC protects a message three ways at once, like a letter written in a code only the reader knows, sent by a trusted route, with the code book locked away.
7.scenario: An Airman's work center handles classified traffic. The encryption equipment is used exactly as its operating instructions say, messages go only over the proper secured system, and the equipment and materials sit in a GSA approved safe inside a secure area. Each habit covers one COMSEC component.
7.example: Writing a valuable letter in code, sending it by a trusted courier and locking the code book away uses three protections at once. COMSEC also combines several protections. In the course: the objective of the COMSEC program is to ensure the employment of measures and controls taken to deny unauthorized persons information derived from information systems of the United States Government related to national security and to ensure the authenticity of such information systems, Block Text p.73.

picture.alt: A message leaves crypto equipment in a secure area over a secured system to a receiver; an enemy intercepts only encrypted signals; COMSEC material sits in a GSA safe.

steps.caption: COMSEC denies unauthorized persons information from U.S. Government information systems related to national security, and ensures their authenticity.
Cryptosecurity: the proper use of cryptographic systems scrambles messages so the enemy cannot decipher intercepted signals.
TRANSEC: protecting transmissions by choosing the right secured system, such as a secure telephone or a cryptographically secured fax.
Physical security: barriers, access only for essential cleared personnel, and a GSA approved safe within a secure area for COMSEC material.

7.summary: Decryption is the restoration of encrypted data to its original plain text or other readily usable state.
7.deeper: Decryption is the partner of encryption, which converts data into a form that cannot be easily understood by unauthorized people; cryptography is the use of coding systems to encrypt and decrypt information. Encrypting data puts the information in an unreadable format until an authorized person decrypts it, which places it back in a readable format. Encryption protects files in storage and in transit across the network. Cryptanalysis is different from decryption: it is the attempt to break a coding system so that the information is revealed to an unauthorized user.
7.analogy: Encryption locks a message in a box; decryption is the owner opening the box with the right key.
7.scenario: An Airman receives an encrypted file over the network. While it travelled, anyone who saw it would have found it unreadable. Once the Airman, an authorized person, decrypts it, the file is back in its original readable form.
7.example: A letter written in a family's private code means nothing to strangers, but a relative who knows the code turns it back into plain words. That turning back is decryption. In the course: decryption is the restoration of encrypted data to its original plain text or other readily usable state, Block Text p.74.

7.summary: Cryptanalysis is the science of trying to break a coding system so that the information can be revealed to an unauthorized user.
7.deeper: Cryptanalysis is one of the key COMSEC terms, with encryption, decryption and cryptography. Enemies cannot always be prevented from intercepting information sent over telecommunications circuits, so our cryptographic systems are meant to defeat the enemy's cryptanalysis efforts: with good cryptosecurity, intercepted messages are scrambled so skillfully that the enemy cannot decipher them. TRANSEC protects transmissions from interception and exploitation by means other than cryptanalysis; it cannot protect against the enemy's cryptanalysis efforts, a task that belongs to cryptosecurity.
7.analogy: Cryptanalysis is the lock-picker's craft: the locked box may already be in the thief's hands, and the work is opening it without the key.
7.scenario: An adversary records signals from a unit's circuit. Keeping the signals away from the adversary was the job of choosing a secured system; now the adversary tries cryptanalysis to break the coding. Because the unit's cryptosecurity is good, the intercepted signals stay unintelligible.
7.example: Someone who finds a diary written in a private code and tries to work out the code is attempting a small version of cryptanalysis. In the course: cryptanalysis is the science of trying to break a coding system so that the information can be revealed to an unauthorized user, Block Text p.74.

7.summary: Cryptosecurity is the protection that results from the proper use of cryptographic systems.
7.deeper: Cryptosecurity is the first COMSEC component. It includes not only creating a highly secure encryption system but also using it properly. Because interception cannot always be prevented, good cryptosecurity scrambles (encrypts) messages so skillfully that the enemy cannot decipher them. Failing to follow the operating instructions that come with cryptographic equipment is a major vulnerability, as is discussing the encryption or decryption process in an unsecured area, over an unsecured telephone or with an unauthorized person. Proper cryptosecurity never bypasses the operational guidance of cryptographic systems and never reveals equipment information such as type, configuration or operational status to an unauthorized person.
7.analogy: A strong lock gives no protection if the door is propped open. Cryptosecurity needs both the strong lock and the habit of using it correctly.
7.scenario: MSgt Rush sees a new Airman skip a step in the crypto equipment's operating instructions to save time, and later hears a caller on an unsecured phone ask how the equipment is configured. Both are cryptosecurity vulnerabilities: the step is never bypassed, and the caller gets no answer.
7.example: A home alarm helps only if it is set the way its instructions say. Cryptosecurity is likewise about proper use as well as a strong system. In the course: cryptosecurity is the protection that results from the proper use of cryptographic systems, Block Text p.74.

7.summary: TRANSEC results from all measures designed to protect intentional transmissions from interception and exploitation by means other than cryptanalysis.
7.deeper: TRANSEC is the second COMSEC component. Cryptosecurity encrypts information so it is protected while it is sent; TRANSEC selects the proper transmission method, making us choose the right secured system for each communications need. It cannot protect against the enemy's cryptanalysis efforts; that task belongs to cryptosecurity. A secure telephone protects verbal information, and a cryptographically secured facsimile system is another method. Vulnerabilities occur when we fail to use the proper system. Since it may be impossible to ensure the enemy will not intercept transmissions, proper cryptosecurity techniques keep intercepted signals unintelligible.
7.analogy: TRANSEC is choosing the armoured van instead of an open bicycle to carry a package: it is about the route and the vehicle, not the lock on the package.
7.scenario: An Airman must pass verbal information about an operation. Instead of an ordinary phone, the Airman uses a secure telephone. To send a document, the Airman uses a cryptographically secured facsimile system.
7.example: Choosing a sealed courier over a postcard for a private note is choosing the right way to send it. TRANSEC is that choice for communications. In the course: TRANSEC results from all measures designed to protect intentional transmissions from interception and exploitation by means other than cryptanalysis, Block Text p.75.

7.summary: In COMSEC, physical security protects COMSEC material against improper destruction of waste, improper handling, and unauthorized viewing or possession.
7.deeper: Physical security is the third COMSEC component. In everyday life it means locking doors and windows and not letting an uninvited stranger in without finding out who they are; in COMSEC it takes on additional threats. Protection comes from physical barriers and from limiting COMSEC access to only essential and properly cleared personnel. COMSEC materials are stored in a GSA approved safe of the appropriate classification, and the safe and any cryptographic equipment are located within a secure area. The authorized personnel for a particular safe are listed on an access control letter created for that safe, and all COMSEC users follow the applicable COMSEC and physical security operating instructions.
7.analogy: It is home security for COMSEC material: strong doors, a short list of who holds a key, and care with what goes out in the trash.
7.scenario: An Airman ending a shift checks that COMSEC waste was destroyed properly, that the safe is locked, and that only people on the safe's access control letter opened it. A visitor without the right clearance waits outside the secure area.
7.example: Locking the doors and windows when you leave home, and not letting a stranger in without knowing who they are, is everyday physical security. In the course: we physically protect against vulnerabilities by creating physical barriers and limiting COMSEC access to only essential and properly cleared personnel, Block Text p.75.

7.summary: Security programs are the Air Force programs that direct the goals and methods for protecting data, information systems, processes and technologies: COMPUSEC, TEMPEST, INFOSEC, OPSEC and COMSEC.
7.deeper: Computer security, information security and communication security are also information technology industry terms; here they name the Air Force programs, and the AF terms and definitions apply. COMPUSEC focuses on end-point security and ports, protocols and services management. TEMPEST identifies vulnerabilities that could lead to compromising emanations and contains those emanations within an inspectable space. INFOSEC identifies and protects classified national security information and CUI. OPSEC reduces adversary collection and exploitation of critical information. COMSEC denies unauthorized persons information from government information systems and ensures their authenticity. Securing data and information is a responsibility that falls on everyone.
7.analogy: The programs are like the different guards of one building: one watches the computers, one the stray signals, one the documents, one what people let slip, and one the communications lines.
7.scenario: An Airman's week touches every program: securing end points (COMPUSEC), keeping equipment emanations within an inspectable space (TEMPEST), marking a CUI document (INFOSEC), keeping deployment dates off social media (OPSEC) and storing crypto material in an approved safe (COMSEC).
7.example: A large organisation may give separate teams the jobs of fire safety, building access and records, each with its own goals. The Air Force divides security into programs in a similar way. In the course: various security programs exist within the Air Force to direct the goals and methods for protecting our data, information systems, processes, and technologies, Block Text p.54.
